Serial learning�refers to the situation where the individual learns a series of responses in a definite order or sequence.�

When the individual masters the serial learning material, then each item becomes a connection or a stimulus for the appearance of the next item because the items are arranged in a prescribed sequence. For example, in chemistry, students need to master how to read the periodic table before they can learn anything else in the course. That's the first part of the series.

The first and last items in the series are learned more easily because they occupy a special position.

The�primacy�effect�refers to the fact that�the first few items are learned the most thoroughly.�For example, people likely remember the nursery rhymes they learned in childhood more easily than the poetry they studied in high school. Ask your parents or grandparents who they remember best: This is also linked to the idea that first impressions of something have quite a dramatic impact.

The�recency�effect�means the last items on the list are the next easiest to learn. �For example, I can remember the first address and telephone number I ever had to learn (that s�primacy) and I can remember my current address and phone number (that s�recency).�I cannot remember the addresses and phone numbers of the places I ve lived in between then and now. The remainder of the items in the middle of the series is learned with the greatest difficulty of all. They seem to have no special significance. �It may be wise to keep this information in mind the next time you have a job interview.�If you have a choice, try to get the first or the last interview, so you stay in the interviewers minds easier.
